title: First bot has been running for almost a month and it's not breached yet!
author: MettleDesk
selftext:
I sat down with an LLM for about 3 straight weeks and hammered out an MGC bot to trade a lucid 50k for shits and giggles. My backtest with the promoted profile achieved a pretty solid result, although I think June and now the start of July 2026 are trying to dissuade me from continuing.

  
These numbers are from my portfolio which is restricted to one position at a time, five potential setup categories, risk up to 2% (for unicorn setups only), and following all of the rules that Lucid has for algo trading. I think this is a gross case of overfit, but after the 10th trading day it hasn't breached yet! Maybe there's some hope for this little clanker after all.

  
Anyway, wanted to check on this sub and see how June/July have been for you guys thus far. It's my first time trading any sort of automation, and I've had an absolute blast getting to this point. If you have any insights based on the screenshots, please let it rip. I'm here to learn and improve, and to hopefully help someone else along the way.

replies.author: MettleDesk
replies.body: My bot is a Python + NinjaTrader automated MGC futures algo. Python handles strategy, risk, journaling, dashboards, and backtesting; NinjaTrader supplies live market/account data and executes trades through custom NinjaScript. It includes a local control app, web dashboard, safety locks, live/preview modes, and setup-performance tracking. Used GPT5.5 quite a bit for building the UI, but strategy and setups were all hand-built from my experience of trading manually for about two years.

replies.author: MettleDesk
replies.body: I used Codex to build it out. The strategy, confirmation, execution all came from my accumulated trading knowledge but the actual software development is what GPT5.5 brought to the table. I was able to for the most part explain the UI in plain english, and with enough time and patience, coaxed the LLM into building a usable dashboard that fit the theme of my journaling/context app that I've also been building this year.

replies.body: Yep, absolutely. Lucid doesn't allow HFT algos, but otherwise they're pretty okay with bots. I'm only using NinjaTrader (as opposed to MT5) because it's available without needing a tradovate API key, which is only available for lucid accounts that have passed eval stage and are funded/live. I do plan to eventually scale to 5 copy accounts once I can pass them all through to Funded and then Live, which allows me to access a tradovate API key and simplify the bot process a bit by removing the NinjaScript part of the process and host the bot on AWS, for instance, rather than running on my desktop pc 24/7.

replies.author: MettleDesk
replies.body:
I'll say that incorporating 5 different setups is the differentiator for my bot's backtest success. It started with my favorite manual strategy in trend pullback, and I saw that to reach the EV I wanted, it would only place a trade every other month or so. I'm picky... So, I struggled through learning how to give it two setups, then three, and now it's constantly scanning for my 5 top setups. Once it finds a good one, it will calculate risk and position based on rules that are specific to the setup it's going with on that particular trade. It was a pain in the ass to figure out how to code, but once I did, it's made all the difference.

  
I'll tell you that my portfolio scans for the following 5 setups at the close of every M15 candle, then evaluates with the strategy that I've developed. The setups are called ORB, PDH Rejection, Trend Continuation, Trend Pullback, and Session Level Reclaim. The fine-tuning of course is the tricky part, but I got the idea from reading books like The Playbook, Technical Analysis Using Multiple Timeframes, and Atomic Habits. I always traded manually by watching for an ORB play at NY open, then depending on price I would swap my chart to watch for Trend Pullback & Continuation, Sweep & Reclaim, or Range Edge Reversal depending on what the market was doing. Having a 'play' for any situation is the idea though, and it translates pretty well into this algo.

The really interesting part is in backtest results. There's usually one setup that is carrying the pack hard for several months at a time, but the best performer rotates in and out depending on the broader market regime around that time. I think that's another hurdle that a lot of bots just don't end up getting past, when the regime changes and your algo doesn't have an answer for it. I'm hoping to avoid that situation with this thing, but time will tell.

replies.author: MettleDesk
replies.body: For the TLDR, I'd recommend some version of Trend Pullback strategies. Something along the lines of 20ma over 50ma over 200ma, clear uptrend, entry on a touch of the 50ma with fading volume, and appropriate bracket positioning. I put up a free indicator called MA Pullback v1.2.1 on tradingview that pairs with my other free volume indicator called MoveProof v3.0 that was pretty effective for me if you want to experience it more.

replies.author: MettleDesk
replies.body: I've tried to give it enough 'plays' to have an answer for everything we've seen since 2010. The strategy layers runs on a 5-family setup filter, so as it's scanning fresh M15 bars on the chart, it's grading the strength of each different setup. Once it sees a match, whether it's ORB, Trend Pullback, or Session Level Reclaim for example, it will execute on that underlying logic and enter a bracketed position with stop and tp1/2/3 based on the supporting factors that price is showing us and variables within each setup family to try and optimize each trade. I will say it's been profitable in backtest every year since 2010, in fact only had a few losing months sprinkled in there.
